Question: Which Arabidopsis flowering-time candidate genes are supported across multiple GWAS studies and deserve priority for validation?
Answer:
**Bottom line:** In the retrieved evidence, no Arabidopsis flowering-time gene is established as replicated across multiple independent GWAS. The strongest cross-study validation priority is **FRI**, with **FLC** a secondary candidate.

**FRI — highest priority.** FRI was detected in genome-wide association mapping under long days without vernalization, where FRI-region associations were consistently among the ten most significant [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0010060). Coding-region deletions at FRI were also replicated in both mapping populations in candidate-gene association mapping [2](https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.109.105189). FRI has additional QTL [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000105) and latitudinal-cline support [4](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0306401101). This is cross-study association/QTL support, but not multiple independent GWAS; in a field-over-winter linkage/association study, FRI functionality did not associate significantly with flowering time [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940).

**FLC — secondary.** Natural FLC allelic variation and functional alleles are documented [6](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.1217304)[7](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0010006). However, in one linkage/association study, no significant FLC haplogroup effect remained after accounting for population structure (−log10 P = 0.07; −log10 P = 0.62 with functional FRI) [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940). FLC therefore warrants structure-controlled validation rather than being treated as a replicated GWAS hit.

**Other candidates.** PHYC has natural-population allelic association with flowering and growth responses [8](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng1818). FLM has a natural deletion associated with flowering-time variation [9](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0409474102) and QTL interaction with FRI [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000105). Neither has multi-GWAS support in the retrieved evidence.

**Local KG GWAS candidates.** The retained Arabidopsis flowering-time GWAS records come from one study (199 accessions; 3VmrMLM; FT10/FT22; PMID 38259933) [10][11]. Its proximity-linked genes—AT1G01540, AT1G01550/BPS1, AT1G05127, and AT1G14880/PCR1—each have a single GWAS link and no additional trait-association or molecular-QTL result [12][13][14][11][15][16]. They are not multi-study priorities without independent replication.

Answer:
**Priority ranking — MSU7 chr5:5,315,122–5,416,701 (±50 kb around GW5)** [1]

1. **GSE5/GW5 — LOC_Os05g09520 (top priority).** This is the anchor gene at chr5:5,365,122–5,366,701 [2]. Functional evidence directly supports grain width: loss of function caused wide, heavy grains, whereas overexpression caused narrow grains; promoter deletions DEL1/DEL2 reduced expression and were associated with wide grains [3](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2017.03.009). GW5/GSE5 has also been linked to brassinosteroid signaling [4](https://doi.org/10.1038/nplants.2017.43) and tested by CRISPR/grain phenotyping [5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00497-018-0333-6)[6](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-024-00728-6), with additional GWAS/QTL support [7](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2020.00395). Use **GSE5** as the summary symbol; the historical 2008 qSW5 deletion subject should not be treated as automatically equivalent [2].

2. **OsDER1 — LOC_Os05g09550 (second priority; 27.6 kb right).** Stored S001_Leaf sQTL records include EWAS associations with grain width (P≈2.58–2.60×10⁻⁵) and grain thickness (P≈9.33×10⁻⁴), plus suggestive Coloc support for grain weight (PP.H4≈0.560) [8]. These are association/splicing signals, not causal proof.

3. **OsHXK7 — LOC_Os05g09500 (lower priority for grain width).** Retrieved literature covers hexokinase localization, sugar signaling, hypoxia and nitrogen use [12](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10535-011-0025-7)[13](https://doi.org/10.1111/jipb.12366)[14](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jplph.2024.154182)[15](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.devcel.2023.06.003)[16](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00425-006-0251-y); one yield-related GWAS/haplotype study [17](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1909754) reports OsHXK7 as one of four prioritized candidate genes within a set of GY/SSR/PH/TGW QTL intervals, not a grain-width-specific finding. No retained PlantQTLdb trait-evidence record was retrieved for this gene [18]. It is a physiological/yield-related candidate, not a grain-width priority on current evidence.

**Unresolved:** No gene-targeted literature retrieval was performed for LOC_Os05g09510, so it remains unranked; the remaining neighbors were not assessed in this review. This ranking is not exhaustive, and the OsDER1 evidence is leaf sQTL/Coloc-based.

Question: What do complementation experiments reveal about the roles of the short and long CPSF30 protein isoforms in Arabidopsis nitrate responses?
Answer:
**Complementation evidence**

The long isoform, **CPSF30-L (65 kDa; AT1G30460)**, complements nitrate-related defects in *cpsf30* mutants. Expression of wild-type 65-kDa CPSF30-L restored nitrate-responsive gene induction in the nitrate-regulatory mutant [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.14743). In *cpsf30-2*, wild-type CPSF30-L rescued defects in alternative polyadenylation and nitrate metabolism, whereas m6A-binding-defective CPSF30-L did not [2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2021.01.013). A review-level summary further reports that a complemented **CPSF30-L/cpsf30-2** line restored nitrate-responsive *NIA1*, *NiR* and *NRT2.1* expression to wild-type levels [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms19072039). CPSF30-L acts upstream of *NRT1.1* and independently of NLP7, and *NRT1.1* 3′-UTR polyadenylation-site patterns were altered in the mutant [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.14743). Thus, the long isoform can restore nitrate signaling/APA defects in the tested mutant backgrounds, and a functional m6A-binding YTH domain is required for the tested rescue.

**Short isoform**

CPSF30-S is the 30-kDa portion of CPSF30-L, which additionally contains the m6A-binding YTH domain [4](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2021.01.014). Retrieved complementation evidence shows that CPSF30 alone restored wild-type growth and oxidative-stress susceptibility to *oxt6* [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0002410), but the retrieved abstract reports growth and oxidative-stress phenotypes, not nitrate responses. No retrieved nitrate-rescue experiment using CPSF30-S alone was found; therefore, the retrieved evidence does not establish whether the short isoform can complement nitrate phenotypes. Complementation demonstrates sufficiency in the mutant background, not exclusive isoform function.

Question: What support do genetic associations and functional experiments each provide for the hypothesis that FLC expression affects Arabidopsis flowering time?
Answer:
## FLC (AT5G10140) and flowering time: association vs. functional evidence

**Genetic/statistical associations (correlative).** In the local PlantQTLdb Arabidopsis KG, FLC has 42 retained trait records, all of them **EWAS** (measured leaf expression vs. trait, 1001 Genomes, dataset S010_Leaf, MOMENT, threshold P ≤ 0.001) — no TWAS, SMR or Coloc record was retained for this gene [1]. Significant EWAS hits include days-to-flowering traits: DTF Sweden 2009 1st experiment (P = 1.14×10⁻⁵, effect 11.32, SE 2.58), DTF Sweden 2009 2nd (P = 1.61×10⁻⁴, effect 16.24), DTF Spain 2008 1st (P = 6.90×10⁻⁴, effect 4.40) [1]. Literature-level association evidence adds an AtMAD TWAS association with DTF Spain 2008 (Pearson 0.62, FDR 0.005) [2](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaa1042), recovery of FLC among top-ranked genes by univariate environmentally predicted trait mapping/GWAS (rank 671 on flowering time; also ranks 617/627 for RF/day length—not a bivariate-ETM recovery) [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005594), and an expression–phenotype correlation of r² = 0.53 [4](https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.118.200571). These establish that FLC transcript level co-varies with flowering time in natural populations; they do not by themselves show that changing FLC expression changes flowering.

**Functional experiments (interventional).** Primary experiments do show direction and mechanism. An FLC:HA fusion binds in vivo the FD and SOC1 promoters and the FT first intron; FLC in the meristem impairs response to the FT signal, and repression at multiple levels is required for the extreme flowering delay it causes [5](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.373506). In transgenic plants overexpressing CO and FLC, the two act antagonistically and FLC blocks CO activation of SOC1 through a CArG box [6](https://doi.org/10.1093/emboj/cdf432). Genetic epistasis places FLC downstream of FRI: FRI function "absolutely requires FLC activity" (FRI flc-3 vs fri-Col flc-3) [7](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0010006). Natural-variation data are consistent: Cph-0 has ~500-fold higher FLC and 1–2% of Col-0 FT transcript and flowers later (41.6 vs 28.4 d) [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2015.00697).

**Limitations.** The EWAS effects are descriptive expression–trait associations in one leaf dataset, not QTLs or causal tests; effect coding is not documented in the retrieved record. Several literature items are extraction notes, and S0044/S0042 were read only as abstracts.

Question: Does Hd1 have the same effect on rice heading across genetic backgrounds, and what evidence explains any differences?
Answer:
## Short answer

No. Hd1's effect on heading is not constant across genetic backgrounds: its **direction** (promotion vs. delay) and its **magnitude** both change, and the best-supported explanation is allelic interaction with the Ghd7/DTH8(PRR37) repressor module plus day length.

## Evidence

**Baseline function is promotion.** In a CRISPR isogenic series in one background, Hd1 promoted flowering "regardless of day-length" when Ghd7 and DTH8 were nonfunctional; in the ghd7/dth8 line Hd1 advanced heading by ~14 d under artificial short days [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.16946). Hd1 alone promotes heading in homozygous line comparisons under both LD and SD [2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jgg.2022.02.018).

**Functional Ghd7/DTH8 convert Hd1 into a net repressor.** Under LD, Hd1 promotes *Ghd7* expression and is recruited by Ghd7 and/or DTH8 into repressive complexes that suppress the Ehd1–Hd3a/RFT1 pathway, blocking heading; under SD, Hd1 competes with these complexes and promotes Hd3a/RFT1 [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.16946). Consequently, in the strong-photoperiod-sensitive NHLD/I7 background, *Hd1* knockout headed early under artificial LD (109.4 d) but was indistinguishable from wild type under natural SD [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.16946). Conversely, an *hd1* null in the japonica Ningjing8 background headed ~31 d earlier than NJ8 at Nanjing [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/pbi.14221).

**Quantitative background dependence.** In a ZS97 near-isogenic four-gene population, Ghd7 explained 58%, 21.7% and 29.1% of heading-date variation in *hd1*, *Hd1H* and *Hd1* classes under natural SD, and the strongest digenic interaction shifted between Ghd7×Ghd8 (NLD) and Ghd7×PRR37 (NSD) depending on Hd1 genotype [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-019-0314-x). PRR37 additive effects ranged from 1.8 to 19.4 d across Ghd7/Ghd8/Hd1 combinations under NLD, whereas under NSD the same gene became a heading activator in some combinations (additive effects as low as −9.9 d) [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-019-0314-x).

**Allele- and germplasm-level differences.** The functional ZS97 *Hd1* allele promoted heading by 4.64–6.14 d under NSD and NLD in the ZS97 background and behaved photoperiod-insensitively [5](https://doi.org/10.1242/bio.021071); in a nonfunctional *ghd7* background it promoted flowering under both NSD and NLD [6](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms20030516). A late-type *Hd1* allele in Fusaotome/Chiba 28 NILs delayed heading by ~13 d [7](https://doi.org/10.1270/jsbbr.22j15). In a 45-accession panel, functional *Hd1* gave very early flowering in natural SD (24.5/24.7 d) with no LD difference under matched genotypes, yet *hd1* GUVA lines flowered ~8.2 d earlier than Korean japonica under natural LD — implying additional, unidentified modifiers [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.01827).

## Limitations

These are different populations, allele contrasts and day-length regimes (natural vs. artificial), so effect sizes are not directly comparable; several records are literature-extraction notes rather than re-read primary text. The "additional genetic factors" beyond Ghd7/DTH8 are proposed, not identified [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.01827).

Question: How strongly does experimental evidence support a role for natural variation in OsHKT1;5 in rice salt tolerance?
Answer:
## Short answer

Evidence is **strong for OsHKT1;5 (LOC_Os01g20160; SKC1/OsHKT8) being required for rice salt tolerance, but only moderate and partly conflicting for the specific claim that *natural* allelic variation at this gene drives tolerance differences in rice germplasm.**

## What is well supported

- **Gene function (strong, experimental):** Two independent T-DNA insertional mutants showed that loss of OsHKT1;5 in salt-stressed roots causes massive shoot Na⁺ accumulation, with ²²Na⁺ tracer evidence for xylem Na⁺ unloading in roots and leaf sheaths and phloem localization in basal nodes [1](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.13595). A CRISPR *hkt1;5* single mutant is salt-sensitive, and an *nac10 hkt1;5* double mutant is comparably sensitive [2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771). These establish function, not natural-variation effects.
- **Natural variation (strongest single case):** The SKC1/qSKC-1 locus was map-based cloned in a Nona Bokra × Koshihikari population and delimited to a 7.4-kb interval; it was identified as OsHKT1;5, a Na⁺-selective transporter underlying a higher shoot K⁺/Na⁺ ratio [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms222111674)[1](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.13595). The QTL was reported to explain ~40.1% of phenotypic variation in the F₂ population [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms222111674). This is the anchor evidence that a naturally occurring allele at this gene affects shoot ion homeostasis.
- **Introgression/breeding evidence:** Improved lines RGD1 and RGD4 carrying SKC1 grew better under salt stress, and introgression of SKC1 was reported to confer salt and drought tolerance [4](https://doi.org/10.4067/s0718-58392022000100097)[5](https://doi.org/10.47836/pjtas.43.4.17). These support a SKC1-containing donor segment in improved rice lines, but the retrieved abstracts do not define the OsHKT1;5 allele or separate it from linked donor variation.

## What is weaker or conflicting

- EcoTILLING of 392 accessions found five nonsynonymous SNPs associated with salt-stress traits, including T67K and P140A in OsHKT1;5 [6](https://doi.org/10.1111/pbi.12010) — association-level, abstract only, no allele-specific functional test retrieved.
- Amino-acid substitutions (140, 184, D332H, V395L) distinguish tolerant from sensitive genotypes across *Oryza* and *P. coarctata*, but the authors state this "will need to be validated experimentally" [7](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2019.01420); it is correlative plus modelling.
- A 29-accession *japonica* panel found **no significant** difference in salt-tolerance score among OsHKT1;5 haplotypes, although tolerant Huangluo had higher root expression than sensitive Shanfuliya [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1095929).

## Limitations

The 40.1% PVE figure comes from a review [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms222111674), not the primary cloning paper. Association studies differ in panel, subspecies, trait and marker, so they are not independent replications. Expression differences are not QTLs. The retrieved records do not establish allele-specific validation by allele-swap/transgenic experiments in a common background; the introgression evidence above does not resolve the causal allele.

Question: How strong is the field evidence that DRO1 improves rice yield under drought?
Answer: ## Short answer The field evidence is **real but narrow**: DRO1 has field support for raising grain yield under drought, but the unconfounded DRO1-alone evidence is essentially one donor/recipient combination (Kinandang Patong allele in the IR64 background); other field material carries DRO1 together with additional QTLs. The retrieved record does not include a multi-environment, multi-year, DRO1-alone field validation in diverse elite backgrounds. ## What the field evidence shows - **Original cloning/validation (Uga et al. 2013, Nat Genet [1](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2725))**: introducing DRO1 from the deep-rooting donor into a shallow-rooting cultivar by backcrossing produced lines that "maintained high yield performance under drought conditions relative to the recipient cultivar." The retrieved text is the abstract only, so no trial numbers, sites or years are available from it. - **Field yield quantification ([2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-015-0049-2), full text)**: this review/background passage states that under upland conditions with drought stress, Dro1-NIL had a significantly higher grain yield than IR64 (citing Uga et al. 2013a), and that in an irrigated paddy field it yielded about 10% more than IR64 (attributed there to Arai-Sanoh et al. 2014), linked to greater post-heading N uptake from deeper soil. This is the clearest retrieved statement of a field yield advantage, but it is a secondary citation and gives no drought effect size. - **Across water regimes ([3](https://doi.org/10.1080/1343943x.2017.1305868))**: a title-level record reports IR64 NILs carrying DRO1 (and STELE TRANSVERSAL AREA 1) improving yield formation across flooded lowland, alternate wetting and drying, and rainfed upland; the "14% higher yield" figure appears only in a literature-extraction note, not in retrieved full text, so treat it as unverified. - **Breeding deployment ([4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-10951-w), full text)**: Maudamani-derived pyramided lines carrying DRO1 + DRO3 + Pup1 out-yielded the recurrent parent in 2024 dry- and wet-season field trials with no yield penalty, but the three QTLs were introgressed together, so this does not isolate a DRO1 effect. ## Limitations Unconfounded evidence is concentrated in the IR64/Kinandang Patong isogenic contrast; the retrieved sources do not establish effect size stability across sites, years or genetic backgrounds, and several supporting statements are review/background citations rather than primary trials. Question: How does WUSCHEL maintain stem cells in the Arabidopsis shoot apical meristem?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## WUSCHEL (AT2G17950) and shoot apical meristem stem cell maintenance

**Where WUS acts.** WUS encodes a homeodomain transcription factor transcribed in a small group of cells — the organizing center (OC) — beneath the stem cells of the shoot apical meristem. WUS protein moves from the OC into the overlying stem cells, where it represses differentiation genes and directly activates *CLAVATA3* (*CLV3*) [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2015248117). A dedicated study of WUS protein movement as the basis of stem cell homeostasis is also recorded in the local literature [2](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.17258511), though only its title was retrievable here.

**The WUS–CLV3 feedback loop.** CLV3 encodes a small peptide that signals back from the stem cells to the OC, delimiting *WUS* expression and thereby limiting stem cell number; reduced CLV3 activity causes stem cell overproliferation, whereas increased CLV3 reduces or abolishes stem cells [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2015248117). This negative feedback loop is the core homeostatic mechanism [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms221910621).

**Partners and cofactors.** WUS physically interacts with SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM); WUS activates *STM* expression, STM binds a *CLV3* promoter motif (−797 to −793), and WUS binds a separate motif (−1082 to −1079); both sites are required for CLV3 expression and stem cell homeostasis, and STM enhances WUS binding at the WUS site [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2015248117). In the OC, HAIRY MERISTEM (HAM1/HAM2) proteins interact with WUS [4](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13853) and can inhibit WUS-mediated CLV3 activation [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2015248117); *wus-7;ham1;2;3* mutants terminate meristems like *wus* nulls [4](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13853).

**Concentration control.** WUS accumulation is patterned by DNA-dependent homodimerization, nuclear–cytoplasmic partitioning and protein destabilization, giving concentration-dependent CLV3 regulation [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007351). Rib-meristem cytokinin signaling stabilizes WUS protein through its acidic domain and WUS-box; cytokinin-receptor mutants accumulate less WUS [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007351).

**Auxin gating.** WUS also acts as an auxin-response rheostat, repressing auxin pathway genes via histone deacetylation and keeping stem cells at low, instructive auxin output while protecting them from auxin-induced differentiation [6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-13074-9).

Question: What roles do SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW play in establishing the tissue layers of Arabidopsis roots?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## SHORT-ROOT (SHR, AT4G37650) and SCARECROW (SCR, AT3G54220) in Arabidopsis root tissue layers

Both are plant-specific GRAS-family transcription factors [1][2]; they act as key regulators patterning the root's radial (concentric) tissue layers [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x).

**The ground-tissue division they control.** In the root meristem, the cortex/endodermis initial (CEI) first divides transversely, and its daughter (CEID) then divides longitudinally to produce the two ground-tissue layers, cortex and endodermis [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x)[4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143). In both *shr* and *scr* loss-of-function mutants this longitudinal asymmetric division does not occur, leaving a single ground-tissue layer [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x)[4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143). The identity of that residual layer differs: in *shr* it has only cortex attributes, whereas in *scr* it has mixed cortex/endodermis identity — so SHR is implicated in endodermis fate specification, whereas SCR is not involved in endodermis specification [4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143).

**Division of labour between the two genes.** SHR is expressed in the stele, and its protein moves into the adjacent CEI layer, where it activates the asymmetric-division programme and endodermis specification [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x)[4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143). SHR directly activates *SCR*, whose expression is strongly reduced in *shr* [4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143). SCR in turn restricts SHR movement to the inner ground-tissue layer that becomes the endodermis [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x), and has been reported to reinforce SHR signalling and inhibit periclinal divisions by maintaining high SHR levels in the endodermis [5](https://doi.org/10.4161/psb.22437). SCR is required for the first asymmetric division but represses subsequent ones: in *scr* the single layer occasionally divides to give a middle-cortex-like layer [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2009.03839.x). SHR additionally regulates stele cell division/specification and stem-cell/QC function [4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040143)[6](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11103-011-9826-5).

**Limitations.** These are mutant and reporter-based findings in *Arabidopsis thaliana* primary roots; several statements (e.g. [5](https://doi.org/10.4161/psb.22437)) were available only at title level.

Question: How does SLAC1 contribute to abscisic acid–induced stomatal closure in Arabidopsis?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## SLAC1 (AT1G12480) in ABA-induced stomatal closure

**Identity.** SLAC1 = *SLOW ANION CHANNEL-ASSOCIATED 1* (AT1G12480, chr1:4,257,268–4,259,300, minus strand; also annotated OZS1/CDI3/RCD3) [1].

**Effector role.** SLAC1 is a guard-cell plasma-membrane slow (S-type) anion channel that generates Cl⁻/nitrate efflux and acts as a key effector of stomatal closure (background description) [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43193-3). Loss of SLAC1 function renders stomata unable to close in response to ABA, CO₂, ozone, light/dark transitions, humidity change, Ca²⁺, H₂O₂ and NO, consistent with SLAC1 being required for guard-cell S-type anion channel function [3](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06608). SLAC1 is likewise required for malate-induced closure [4](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.18400), and systems modelling of the Cl⁻-channel (*slac1*) mutant implicates an emergent homeostatic network that regulates K⁺ channels and transpiration [5](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.112.207704).

**Position in ABA signalling.** ABA binding to PYR/PYL receptors sequesters PP2Cs, releasing OST1/SnRK2 kinases, which phosphorylate SLAC1 (e.g. S120) to activate anion efflux [6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518134122). A Ca²⁺-dependent arm converges on the same channel: OST1 phosphorylates CPK15 at Thr103, and CPK15 phosphorylates eight SLAC1 N-terminal residues (S6, S55, S59, T62, S65, S86, S113, S120). The phospho-null SLAC1-8A fails to rescue ABA insensitivity of *slac1-3*, whereas the phosphomimetic SLAC1-7A-T62D variant largely restores closure, identifying T62 as the dominant site; *ost1 cpk15* double mutants are more ABA-insensitive than either single mutant [6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518134122). CPK21 and CPK23 have been shown to phosphorylate SLAC1/SLAHs in vitro, whereas CPK3/4/6/11/21 are implicated in Ca²⁺-dependent activation of SLAC1/SLAHs and cpk3/4/5/6/11 mutants show only partial ABA insensitivity [6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518134122).

**Limitations.** Most statements here come from literature-KG extraction records, several of them background descriptions (e.g. [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43193-3)); only [6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518134122) was examined as a full-text primary paper for the ABA mechanism. The Nature 2008 record [3](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06608) was available only as title/metadata, so its extracted statements were not checked against the original text. The CPK15 study further suggests that SLAH3-type channels may redundantly contribute to ABA-induced closure, because SLAC1-8D did not fully rescue *cpk15-1* [6](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2518134122); this is a proposed redundancy rather than a demonstrated absolute compensation in the retrieved ABA experiments.

Question: How does GS3 regulate grain length in rice?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer: ## GS3 as a negative regulator of rice grain length **Identity and core function.** GS3 is the major grain-length/grain-weight QTL on chromosome 3 (minor QTL for width and thickness), encoding a putative transmembrane protein with a plant-specific organ-size-regulation (OSR) domain; it acts as a **negative regulator** of grain length [1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00122-006-0218-1)[2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e27139). At the cellular level it is reported to limit cell number in the upper epidermis of the glumes [2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e27139). **Signalling mechanism.** GS3 is a Gγ subunit. It reduces grain length not by acting alone but through **competitive binding of the Gβ subunit RGB1**, antagonising DEP1/GGC2–Gβ complexes that promote length, with OsMADS1 (qLGY3) as a downstream effector [2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e27139). Its C-terminal tail restrains the N-terminal domain, and the RING E3 ligase CLG1 ubiquitinates GS3, targeting it for endosomal degradation and thereby increasing grain size [3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-022-00549-5)[2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e27139). **Allelic effects (natural variation).** In the full-text allelic analysis, a C→A substitution in exon 2 (C165A) truncates the protein and is associated with longer, thinner grain; the dominant C allele confers short grain and complemented the long-grain phenotype in transformation tests [4](https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.109.103002). An extraction note for [5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00122-008-0913-1) states the opposite direction (C genotype longer on average than A), but its original text is unavailable in the supplied packet, so this conflict is unresolved. In NILs, loss of GS3 raised grain length from 8.5 to 10.2 mm; two-way ANOVA reported GS3 (P = 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁵), qGL3 (P = 3.71 × 10⁻¹³) and qGL3×GS3 interaction (P = 1.27 × 10⁻⁸) terms, with the authors concluding additive effects were larger than the interaction [6](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12870-015-0515-4). CRISPR knockout of GS3 increased grain length [7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00122-024-04627-8). **Post-transcriptional fine-tuning.** GS3 is alternatively spliced: GS3.1 is the negative regulator (overexpression reduced grain length 8.0%), whereas the abundant truncated GS3.2 has no effect on its own and attenuates GS3.1 by competing more strongly for RGB1 [3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-022-00549-5). **Caveats.** Several records are extraction notes or title-only [1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00122-006-0218-1)[5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00122-008-0913-1); the GS3.1 *isoform* [3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-022-00549-5) is not the separately named QTL "GS3.1" [8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-021-02686-x). Question: How does OsHKT1;5 regulate sodium accumulation in rice shoots?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## OsHKT1;5 (LOC_Os01g20160; SKC1/OsHKT8) and shoot Na⁺ accumulation

**Core mechanism (retrieval from xylem Na⁺).** OsHKT1;5 encodes a class-I HKT Na⁺-selective transporter that is predominantly localized in xylem parenchyma cells and retrieves Na⁺ from the xylem sap, thereby reducing Na⁺ delivery to the shoot — a mechanism described as analogous to AtHKT1;1 [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771). Consistent with this, NMT measurements showed lower net Na⁺ flux in xylem parenchyma cells of Cr-oswrky53 (higher OsHKT1;5 activity) and higher flux in OsWRKY53-OE (lower activity), interpreted as OsHKT1;5-mediated Na⁺ transport from the xylem stream into parenchyma cells of the root elongation zone [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-39167-0). OsHKT1;5 has also been reported to mediate Na⁺ transport in xylem and phloem parenchyma, and the OsNAC10 study links it to shoot-to-root Na⁺ recirculation, which would further limit shoot Na⁺ [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771)[2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-39167-0). The gene was originally identified through the SKC1 QTL affecting the shoot K⁺/Na⁺ ratio [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771).

**Genetic evidence that the transporter limits shoot Na⁺.** In CRISPR–Cas9 experiments in Nipponbare under 75 mM NaCl, *hkt1;5* mutants accumulated the highest shoot Na⁺ and lowest shoot K⁺ among the genotypes tested, and the *hkt1;5* single mutant was salt-sensitive; the *nac10 hkt1;5* double mutant was as salt-sensitive as *hkt1;5*, i.e. loss of OsHKT1;5 was epistatic to *nac10* [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771). Elevated OsHKT1;5 expression (in *nac10* mutants) lowered shoot Na⁺ and xylem-sap Na⁺ and improved salt tolerance, whereas reduced expression (OsNAC10 overexpression) raised shoot Na⁺ [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771).

**Transcriptional control.** OsNAC10 binds an ACGTA core motif in the OsHKT1;5 promoter and competitively represses it under salt stress [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771); OsWRKY53 binds W-box elements in the same promoter, trans-represses OsHKT1;5, and *oswrky53* mutants show enhanced salt-induced root OsHKT1;5 expression and higher OsHKT1;5 activity [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-39167-0).

**Limitations.** These are rice (Nipponbare/ZH11) seedling, hydroponic salt-stress experiments; the vascular/reproductive-tissue protection study [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.13595) was represented here only by title-level metadata and an extracted abstract statement, not full text, and several other retrieved records are background/review statements rather than gene-specific experiments.

The retrieved PlantQTLdb reference record identifies **SVP/AT2G22540** as a protein-coding gene on chromosome 2 (9,579,647–9,583,901, plus strand), but the returned record is gene-level only and does not include transcript IDs, exon counts, exon lengths, or splice coordinates [1]. Question: How do the annotated transcripts of Arabidopsis FCA differ in their coding regions and 3′ UTRs?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## FCA (AT4G16280) transcript variants: coding regions and 3′ UTRs

**What the reference record establishes.** The local Arabidopsis reference annotation [1] places FCA at chr4:9,206,597–9,214,981 (minus strand), locus type protein_coding, description "flowering time control protein FCA". That record contains gene-level coordinates and cross-references only — it returned **no per-transcript exon/intron or UTR models**, so exact annotated transcript structures (exon counts, UTR lengths, CDS boundaries) are not established by the retrieved annotation.

**What the literature establishes.** The two major FCA transcripts described in the literature arise through alternative cleavage and polyadenylation [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/cr.2015.77):
- **FCA-γ** — full-length, functional isoform, polyadenylated at the **distal** site, i.e. using the downstream 3′ UTR [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/cr.2015.77).
- **FCA-β** — truncated, non-functional isoform, polyadenylated at a **proximal** site located **within the third intron** [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/cr.2015.77). Because cleavage occurs in intron 3, this transcript terminates before the downstream coding exons (an inference consistent with the source's "truncated" description); its 3′-terminal region is intronic rather than the canonical 3′ UTR.

This intron-3 proximal site is the basis of FCA autoregulation: FCA promotes polyadenylation of its own pre-mRNA within intron 3 to form FCA-β [3](https://doi.org/10.1071/fp04245) (extraction note). Direct RNA sequencing independently recovered FCA among 104 protein-coding genes with cleavage sites in introns upstream of 3′ UTRs, including the FCA/FPA autoregulatory sites [4](https://doi.org/10.1038/nsmb.2345).

**Regulation of the choice.** HLP1 binds the FCA 3′ UTR and third intron; in *hlp1-1*, third-intron retention increases and distal poly(A) usage falls, reducing FCA-γ [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/cr.2015.77). PCFS4 likewise alters FCA alternative processing [5](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2008.03455.x). Separately, FCA translation initiates at a non-canonical CUG codon [6](https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.067983.118) (background).

**Limitations.** No transcript-resolved annotation was retrieved, so precise CDS/UTR coordinates and lengths remain unresolved; several supporting records were readable only as titles/extraction notes.

Question: How does DOG1 expression change during seed maturation and after imbibition in Arabidopsis?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## DOG1 (AT5G45830) expression across maturation and imbibition

**During seed maturation — transcript declines, protein accumulates.** In wild-type Col-0, qRT-PCR in the HD2A/HD2B study showed that DOG1 mRNA accumulation *decreased from 12 DAP until seed maturation*, consistent with earlier reported Col-0 data cited in that study [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899). The timing of the peak is accession-dependent: in the highly dormant Cvi accession DOG1 expression rose during seed development, peaked at ~16 DAP and then declined, whereas in low-dormant Col it peaked at ~9 DAP and declined to maturity [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899). Maturation environment modulates the level: low temperature during seed maturation increased DOG1 transcript and was associated with deeper dormancy [2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-294x.2011.05181.x)[3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005737). At the protein level, the background of [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899) reports (citing Nakabayashi et al. 2012) that DOG1 protein accumulates during maturation and peaks in freshly harvested seeds, where its level sets dormancy depth.

**Around harvest and after imbibition — a dry-seed peak, then rapid loss.** DOG1 transcript rose rapidly again in dry seeds and then "quickly vanished after seed imbibition" in wild type [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899). In the *hd2ahd2b* mutant, transcript instead kept rising through maturation, peaked in dry seed, and after an initial drop did not vanish but stayed at a relatively stable level for at least 24 h of imbibition [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899). During dry storage, a separate study reports RT-qPCR down-regulation of DOG1 in after-ripened Col seeds [4](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1785818); in the supplied excerpt of that study, the RNA-seq data did not indicate differential DOG1 expression in Col, so the transcript evidence is not uniform. The protein is reported to persist through dry storage and imbibition even as dormancy is lost [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1124899) (background).

**Limitations.** These are transcript measurements in specific accessions/mutants plus protein statements quoted from cited literature; absolute levels, tissues and imbibition conditions differ between studies, and the retrieved passages do not provide a single dataset profiling both mRNA and protein across maturation and imbibition.

Question: How does temperature affect FLM alternative splicing in Arabidopsis?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## FLM alternative splicing responds to ambient temperature in Arabidopsis

**Gene identity:** FLM = AT1G77080 (MAF1/AGL27), chr1, + strand [1].

**Core observation.** FLM pre-mRNA is alternatively spliced, and the two main products, FLM-β and FLM-δ, differ by a mutually exclusive exon (MXE) event [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0172950). In wild-type plants the balance shifts with temperature: FLM-β rises at cool temperature and FLM-δ at warm temperature. In one study the FLM-β/FLM-δ ratio was 7.4, 1.9 and 0.7 at 16, 23 and 27 °C respectively [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2020.596354). A transcriptome-wide shift experiment (23 °C → 27 °C and 23 °C → 16 °C, 24 h) found the FLM MXE event differentially spliced in both directions, i.e. reciprocally [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0172950). After a 16 °C → 25 °C shift, increased retention of FLM's second intron and an MXE event were detected; intron-2 retention yields an NMD-targeted transcript, reducing functional protein at higher temperature [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-017-1235-x). Consistent with this, high temperature is reported to down-regulate FLM through splicing-coupled NMD [5](https://doi.org/10.1038/nplants.2016.55).

**Functional meaning.** FLM-β is the repressive isoform (bound by SVP), so warming reduces repressor output and accelerates flowering [6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-17896-w)[7](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2024.100814). Natural variation can rewire this: the Can-0 SNP28958 in intron 2 creates a splice acceptor, adding 17 nt and a premature stop codon, lowering FLM-β and may desensitize thermosensitivity [6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-17896-w).

**Regulators reported.** AtSF1 binds FLM branch-point/polypyrimidine sequences in introns 1–2 and is required for the temperature-dependent FLM-β/FLM-δ shift (atsf1-2 abolishes the ratio change) [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2020.596354); H3K36me3 writers SDG8/SDG26 are needed for temperature-induced FLM splicing [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-017-1235-x); CDKG2/CYCL1, CRY2–CIS1, AFC2 and NAT10-mediated ac4C are also implicated [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2019.01680)[9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-34886-2)[10](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2022.104051)[11](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.devcel.2025.07.003).

**Limitations.** Temperature regimes, tissues and genotypes differ between studies; several mechanistic claims come from extraction previews or title-level records [12](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12633)[11](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.devcel.2025.07.003)[5](https://doi.org/10.1038/nplants.2016.55) rather than read full text, and no single study establishes the complete causal chain.

**Direct answer:** Within the local rice literature knowledge graph, I found **no record describing alternative splicing of rice *Hd1* (LOC_Os06g16370)** — no intron retention, exon skipping, alternative 5′/3′ splice site use, or alternative transcript isoform of the rice gene is documented in the retrieved evidence. - **The retrieved DCL1 alleles are named laboratory mutant alleles and are not reported as natural accession variants**, and none is described as a splice-site lesion: *dcl1-5* (null, embryo lethal) [3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00497-025-00531-3), *dcl1-7* (point mutation in the RNA-helicase domain) [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12870-015-0533-2), *dcl1-9* (hypomorphic) [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1002035), *dcl1-13* (reported as a dominant suppressor) [6](https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.1297109), *dcl1-14* (weak allele) [7](https://doi.org/10.1093/plcell/koab280).
- **An intronic feature of DCL1** is reported (a miRNA mapping within a DCL1 intron, suggested autoregulation) [8](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.1476406), but this is not a variant annotation.

**Limitations:** I could not access variant-effect annotation records (e.g., VEP-style "splice_donor/splice_acceptor/splice_region" calls) or population polymorphism data in this session, so the specific variants, their coordinates, alleles and carrier accessions cannot be reported. Establishing them would require a variant-annotation/polymorphism resource for *A. thaliana* accessions, which was outside the scope of the tools used here.

Question: Is there GWAS evidence for shade responses within PHYC or 50 kb on either side in Arabidopsis?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

Yes — associations were reported within a ±20 kb window around PHYC, which lies inside your ±50 kb window; the full ±50 kb window was not reported, and the associated phenotype is hypocotyl height rather than the shade-avoidance response itself.

**Evidence retrieved**

- The Arabidopsis shade-avoidance GWAS of Filiault et al. (PLoS Genet, PMID 22438834) explicitly tested the region around PHYC (AT5G35840, chr5:14,007,812–14,011,848, [1]). Significant SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with PHYC were detected by Kruskal–Wallis, with a maximum −log10 P of **4.83 in a ±20 kb window** around the gene; the same SNPs were **not significant under EMMA**, though their P values were elevated relative to flanking SNPs [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002589).
- Genotyping the previously identified PHYC variant (from Balasubramanian et al.) in the same panel gave −log10 P = **4.43 (KW)** and **1.72 (EMMA)** for hypocotyl height in high R:FR (Table 2) [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002589). The authors treated this as confirmation that the KW scan captured true signal.
- The associated phenotype is **hypocotyl height under high R:FR**, not the low R:FR shade-avoidance response. PHYC is not listed in the a priori candidate-gene response-pattern table, whereas PHYB has a KW response value of 6.18 and pattern category 2 [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002589); the retrieved PHYC association is with high R:FR height.

**Limitations**

- The retrieved GWAS used a **±20 kb** window, so it does not establish whether associations extend to 50 kb on either side; no record covering a 50 kb window was retrieved, and this is not evidence of absence.
- The PHYC signal is method-dependent (KW significant, EMMA not), and the authors themselves suggest EMMA may have over-corrected.
- Other PHYC literature retrieved concerns flowering time/climate clines, mutant shade phenotypes (e.g., phyAphyCphyD chlorophyll a/b, [3](https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/ern364)) and QTL mapping near PHYC [4](https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.103.024810) — these are not GWAS shade-response associations.

Question: Do SD1 apaQTLs colocalize with plant-height GWAS signals in rice?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

No retrieved record establishes that SD1 (*OsGA20ox2*; LOC_Os01g66100) apaQTLs colocalize with plant-height GWAS signals in rice. This is an unresolved question in the present evidence, not a demonstrated absence.

## What the evidence does support

- **Gene identity:** SD1 resolves to LOC_Os01g66100 (Os01g0883800) on chromosome 1, annotated as GA 20-oxidase2 [1].
- **SD1–plant height link is well documented**, including mutant/CRISPR and haplotype studies [2](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2024.1333191), [3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-019-1919-x), [4](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms21176170), [5](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2021.714066), [6](https://doi.org/10.1111/pbi.13087), and GWAS-based work: a combined GWAS/epistasis study of Asian cultivated rice is recorded as reporting an SD1 structural variant as a height-associated signal not normally detected in standard GWAS (extraction record; original text unavailable) [7](https://doi.org/10.1111/pce.14557), and SD1 appears in GWAS records for plant height [8](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2016.01801), [9](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms1467). These are trait–gene/GWAS associations, not apaQTL evidence.
- **APA is studied in rice generally** (e.g., subspecies-divergent APA [10](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.14209)). A genome-wide rice APA study reported that APA genes were enriched in QTL regions compared with random regions, but this is a genome-wide QTL enrichment analysis, not an SD1 apaQTL or a test against plant-height GWAS peaks [11](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.210757.116). None of the retrieved records reports an SD1 apaQTL or tests its overlap with height GWAS peaks.

## Why it cannot be answered here

No SD1 apaQTL record or plant-height GWAS–apaQTL colocalization test was retrieved here; targeted literature queries for "apaQTL" and for SD1 with polyadenylation/3′UTR returned no records. This retrieval result does not establish that such analyses were never performed — their outcome is unknown in the supplied evidence. The retrieved evidence is local literature and identifier resolution only.

## What would be needed

An observed SD1 apaQTL (variant coordinates, APA phenotype, tissue, population) plus a plant-height GWAS signal in the same panel, with an explicit overlap/colocalization test. Coordinate overlap alone would not establish allele identity or causality.

Question: Which natural variants in COLD1 are associated with differences in chilling tolerance between indica and japonica rice?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## COLD1 natural variants and indica–japonica chilling tolerance

**Gene identity:** COLD1 = LOC_Os04g51180 (Os04g0600800), chr4:30,311,519–30,316,303 (−), annotated "Regulator of G-protein signaling, Chilling tolerance" [1].

**The principal natural variant.** The principal associated polymorphism is a single nonsynonymous SNP in the fourth exon, originally designated SNP2 (A/T). The japonica allele encodes Lys187, whereas the indica allele encodes Met187/Thr187 [2](https://doi.org/10.5010/jpb.2024.51.029.294). At SNP2, the A state occurs in japonica and T/C in indica and *O. nivara*, with the C state detected in only a small number of accessions (7.8%, 10/127), mostly from India [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants12010215). The japonica (K187) form was associated with chilling tolerance at the seedling stage, whereas indica-type M187/T187 haplotypes were reported as chilling-sensitive; this variant was reported to distinguish cold-tolerant from cold-sensitive accessions and to have been selected during japonica domestication [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants12010215). Loss of COLD1(jap) function or downregulation makes lines cold-sensitive, and overexpression of COLD1(jap) increases chilling tolerance [4](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2015.01.046)[5](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms231810739).

**Independent haplotype survey (3K-RG panel).** Three nonsynonymous SNPs were found in COLD1 coding sequence; K187M was again the key variant, with Lys187-containing haplotypes Hap3 and Hap10 predominantly japonica, while Tongil-type (indica-type) varieties such as Milyang23, Hanareum4 and Geumgang carried Hap1 [2](https://doi.org/10.5010/jpb.2024.51.029.294). Nipponbare and the cold-tolerant Jinbu both fall in Hap3 [2](https://doi.org/10.5010/jpb.2024.51.029.294).

**Functional context.** COLD1 acts in the plasma membrane/ER with RGA1 to activate Ca²⁺ channels and G-protein GTPase activity, and lies within the CSSL4-1 substitution segment underlying subspecies chilling-tolerance divergence [6](https://doi.org/10.1111/jipb.12852)[7](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2021.109397).

**Limitations.** The K187M SNP is highly specific but not sufficient: only 19.6% (9/46) of highly cold-tolerant accessions in one 187-accession panel carried the tolerant allele, with no highly sensitive accession carrying the tolerant allele, so the marker misses many cold-tolerant accessions and other loci contribute to cold tolerance in this panel; the retrieved evidence does not quantify how much of the indica–japonica difference this SNP explains [3](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants12010215). A 2025 study targeting germination-stage cold tolerance reported higher seedling survival for Hap2 (62.76%) than Hap1 (55.88%) and Hap3 (48.25%) (P < 0.01), but its haplotype labels come from a different panel and are not directly comparable to the 3K-RG Hap labels; this is available only as an extraction note here, not verified full text [8](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gene.2025.149600).

Question: Which genes in the Arabidopsis HKT1 region, including 50 kb on either side, have the strongest evidence for leaf-sodium variation?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Answer

Within ±50 kb of *HKT1* (AT4G10310; chr4:6,391,854–6,395,922 [+ strand] [1], i.e. roughly chr4:6.34–6.45 Mb), the gene with by far the strongest retrieved evidence for leaf‑sodium variation is **HKT1 itself**. The only other annotated gene I resolved inside that window, **NIP5;1 (AT4G10380; chr4:6,431,161–6,435,396 [2], ~35 kb from the *HKT1* end), has no retrieved sodium evidence** — its local records concern boric‑acid/boron transport [3](https://doi.org/10.1093/pcp/pcn168)[4](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaf159).

**HKT1 evidence (leaf Na⁺)**
- GWAS of leaf Na⁺ in 337 accessions found a single strong peak centred on AtHKT1;1; the top SNP Chr4:6392276 (T vs C) separated 2,325 vs 955 mg Na⁺ kg⁻¹ DW (p<2e‑16) and explained 32% of total leaf‑Na⁺ variation without accounting for population structure [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1001193).
- Independent F2 QTLs for leaf/shoot Na⁺ centred on AtHKT1;1 in Ts‑1 × Col‑0 and Tsu‑1 × Col‑0, plus deficiency‑complementation tests with *hkt1‑1*, established the locus as causal for the natural high‑Na⁺ phenotype [6](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0020210)[5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1001193).
- The mechanism is cis‑regulatory: "HLS" alleles with low root expression give high leaf Na⁺, and this trade‑off is maintained in coastal populations [7](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1816964115).

**Important caveat on "strongest"**
In MAGIC‑line mapping, the linkage QTL peak for sodium lay 128 kb from AtHKT1 and the strongest GWAS association 8 kb away [8](https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/eraf142). That 8‑kb SNP is inside the 50‑kb window, but the retrieved text does not name the gene at that position, so it cannot be credited to a specific neighbouring gene.

**Scope limits:** this is a local literature‑KG assessment only (no multi‑omics or online searches). The absence of a sodium record for NIP5;1 is a retrieval gap, not evidence that it does not affect leaf Na⁺.

Question: Which Arabidopsis flowering-time candidate genes are supported across multiple GWAS studies and deserve priority for validation?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Cross-study GWAS support for Arabidopsis flowering-time candidates

**Best-supported candidate: ETC3 (AT4G01060).** In the field GWA + linkage study of 197 accessions and 13 RIL families, ETC3 was one of only four genes detected by *both* EMMA and Wilcoxon and additionally confirmed by an overlapping QTL [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940). The same paper notes that ETC3 (and ATGA20X7) had also been proposed as flowering-time candidates in greenhouse GWA mapping of the Atwell et al. panel — i.e. support from a separate study under different conditions [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940). This is the clearest case of convergent GWAS evidence in the retrieved corpus.

**FLC (AT5G10140) — multi-study signal but contested.** FLC was among the top-20 network-boosted candidates for days-to-flowering (LD) and was recoverable from the original GWAS signal alone [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-21301-4). However, araGWAB re-analysed the same 107-phenotype (Atwell) GWAS data, so this is not an independent cohort. In the field GWA study, FLC was *not* confirmed, and no FLC haplogroup effect survived structure correction (−log10 P = 0.07 overall; 0.62 with functional FRI) [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940).

**FRI — detected but not replicated.** FRI associations were "invariably among the ten most significant" in a 95-accession GWA scan, with unique haplotype clusters distinguishing it from structure-driven false positives [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0010060). Yet FRI functionality did not associate significantly with field flowering time over winter (EMMA −log10 P < 2.4 within ±20 kb) [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940).

**PHYD (AT4G16250)** was the only one of the previously functionally validated greenhouse candidates confirmed by GWA in the field study [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000940), but no second GWAS record was retrieved.

**Single-study only:** ATX2, ATX1 and NPF5.15 come from one study's three Cape Verde/Morocco populations, not independent studies [4](https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msad185).

**Limitations:** this is a bounded local-literature retrieval, not an exhaustive GWAS census; absence of a second record is not evidence of no replication. Priority for validation: ETC3 first, then FLC/FRI with explicit structure-controlled, multi-environment designs.

Question: Which rice grain-thickness candidate genes would you prioritize based on associations with poly(A)-site usage?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

No rice grain-thickness candidate can currently be prioritized on poly(A)-site-usage (APA/3′aQTL) evidence. In the retrieved local-literature records, no record links any grain-thickness gene to a poly(A)-site-usage association, so a ranking on that criterion is not supported. This is a bounded search result, not a demonstrated absence: no retrieved record supplies 3′aQTL/apaQTL statistics for these genes, and the outcome of any such analysis is unknown.

## What the retrieved evidence does establish

**Grain-thickness candidates with gene-specific phenotypic support** (useful as the test set, not as APA-prioritized genes):
- **OsETR4 / LOC_Os07g15540** – candidate for *qGV7-2*; Ludao-allele NILs were 6.53% thicker under Nanjing conditions [1](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1579589).
- **OsSPL4 / LOC_Os02g07780** – grain thickness decreased in *spl4-d3* and *spl4-d15* mutants [2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-021-00531-7).
- **OsSRS3 / LOC_Os05g06280** – grain thickness increased 12.77% in the reported mutant analysis [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0338401).
- **GS3 / Os03g0407400** – minor QTL for width and thickness; *gs3* NIL grains 0.07 mm thicker [4](https://doi.org/10.1002/pld3.417)[5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0122206).

**APA-related records exist, but for other traits/genes:** the only APA/QTL record retrieved is a pan-genome APA study on **salt tolerance**, not grain thickness [6](https://doi.org/10.1111/jipb.70399). Its abstract-level extraction reports functional validation of *OsMyb21* and *OsRNS3* as 3′aQTL-associated genes, but in the supplied evidence this source is available at title level only (no retrievable text), so the gene-level details rest on extraction notes and were not verified against the paper.

**Closest indirect leads (3′-UTR sequence variants, not poly(A)-site usage):** a 3′-UTR miRNA-binding-site SNP in *CYP704A3* associated with grain size [7](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12870-016-0779-3)[8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00497-018-0333-6), and the miR156 site in the *GLW7/OsSPL13* 3′-UTR, which comes from review-level background rather than a primary experiment [9](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2021.605799). *OsSPL4* additionally shows heat-stress differential **alternative splicing** [10](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants10081647) — a different molecular layer from APA.

## Limitation

These are unassessed, not negative, for APA: no supporting record was retrieved, and the analysis outcome for grain thickness is unknown. Several other APA-related records in the retrieved set (stress- and development-focused APA studies) were not read, so they neither support nor exclude an APA–thickness link for these genes. Prioritization would require an explicit 3′aQTL/APA–thickness association test in the relevant tissue and population.

Question: Which rice grain-width candidates would you prioritize based on associations with poly(A)-site usage?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

No rice record in the retrieved local literature KG directly links poly(A)-site (PAS) usage to grain width, so a PAS-based ranking cannot be made from evidence. The defensible prioritization is by **3′-UTR variant–grain-width association**, which is a relevant but indirect starting point: a 3′-UTR variant can be tested for effects on PAS choice, but the retrieved associations do not themselves measure PAS usage. On that basis the order is:

**1. LOC_Os11g48090 (helicase C-terminal domain protein) — highest priority.** In a 591-accession 3K-genome panel, two adjacent SNPs 7 bp apart in its 3′-UTR were the only SNPs in this region implicated by LD with raw grain width in japonica (snp11_28989509, −log10P = 9.3, effect 0.94; snp_11_28989516, −log10P = 11.36, effect 1.02); the wide-grain haplotype averaged 2.9 mm vs 2.5 mm [1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-12778-6). The authors *hypothesize* the substitutions disrupt a repressor-binding site (homology to AHL12/AHL25 sites) — a hypothesis they state requires further functional validation; the retrieved evidence does not report a PAS measurement.

**2. LOC_Os07g37920 (NAC transcription factor) — second candidate.** Two non-synonymous SNPs plus a 3′-UTR indel associated with raw grain width (snp_07_22756160; effect 0.22, −log10P = 4.15), a lower reported −log10P in a targeted-gene association within the same study, below the study's −log10P >5 threshold and from a different analysis/population scope than the japonica GWAS signal, so the two P values are not directly comparable [1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-12778-6).

**Mechanistic precedent, not a width candidate:** the *sdt* allele acts through alternative 3′-polyadenylation of the OsmiR156h precursor (LOC_Os06g44034), shortening its 3′-UTR and raising miR156h; but the reported grain phenotype includes *smaller* grains in the WD44-sdt comparison; 1,000-grain weight is reported as reduced there but higher in the NIL-OsSPL14 WFP/sdt table, and grain width is not separately reported in the retrieved passages [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126154).

## Limitations

Apart from the 3′-UTR grain-width associations above, the retrieved APA-related records concern other contexts, such as salt tolerance (OsMyb21, OsRNS3) [3](https://doi.org/10.1111/jipb.70399) and OsmiR156h grain yield [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126154), and do not report grain-width PAS associations. 3′-UTR SNPs, miRNA-site variants (e.g. CYP704A3 [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12870-016-0779-3)) and UTR polymorphisms are not evidence of PAS usage. These candidates are therefore unassessed for PAS usage in the retrieved evidence; the ranking reflects the reported 3′-UTR/grain-width associations and UTR location, not PAS-usage measurements.

Question: What do complementation experiments reveal about the roles of the short and long CPSF30 protein isoforms in Arabidopsis nitrate responses?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
**Complementation evidence indicates that the long CPSF30 isoform, CPSF30-L, is the nitrate-relevant form.** In *cpsf30-2*, induction of nitrate-responsive genes such as *NIA1*, *NiR*, and *NRT2.1* was reduced, and this was restored to wild-type levels in a complemented **CPSF30-L/cpsf30-2** line [1](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms19072039). CPSF30-L complementation also restored *CIPK8* and *CIPK23* expression in the *cpsf30* mutant under nitrate conditions [2](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.00593). An abstract-level extraction further reports that wild-type CPSF30-L rescued alternative polyadenylation and nitrate-metabolism defects in *cpsf30-2*, whereas m6A-binding-defective CPSF30-L variants did not [3](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2021.01.013), implicating the long isoform’s m6A-reader function.

**The short isoform, CPSF30-S, is not supported as the nitrate-response complementing isoform.** The retrieved full text states that CPSF30-L, and not CPSF30-S, was responsible for nitrate signaling, while CPSF30-S interacts with FIP1 and has documented roles in developmental processes and global poly(A) site choice [2](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.00593). Thus, the complementation data support a specific role for CPSF30-L in nitrate signaling and APA of nitrate-related transcripts, including *NRT1.1*.

**Limitation:** the retrieved passages clearly show long-isoform rescue, but the primary short-isoform complementation result is not displayed; the “not CPSF30-S” conclusion comes from a full-text statement citing earlier work [2](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.00593).

Question: What support do genetic associations and functional experiments each provide for the hypothesis that FLC expression affects Arabidopsis flowering time?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## FLC (AT5G10140) and flowering time: what genetic associations vs. functional experiments each show

**Genetic associations (natural variation, correlative)**
- Across 132 Swedish inbred lines, FLC transcript level was the strongest expression correlate of flowering time (Spearman ρ = 0.63, P = 3.05E-16; r² = 0.53) [1](https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.118.200571).
- A GWAS in the same panel found a genome-wide significant SNP in the FLC promoter (Chr5:3,180,721; P = 1.14E-08, MAF 0.38) for flowering time; a mediation model with this SNP plus FLC expression explained r² = 0.48 of flowering variation (expression r² = 0.29, SNP r² = 0.19) [1](https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.118.200571).
- An expression–phenotype association resource (AtMAD, correlation-based "TWAS") reports FLC–days-to-flowering in the Spain-2008 trial (Pearson 0.62, FDR 0.005) [2](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaa1042).
- In a Col-0 × Cph-0 QTL cross, FLC fell under a major flowering QTL, with FLC ~500-fold higher and FT at 1–2% in the late Cph-0 parent [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2015.00697).

**Functional experiments (perturbation, causal test)**
- A T-DNA FLC knockout (flc-7, no transcript) flowered with 8.45 ± 0.19 leaves; introducing flc-7 into the late-flowering p5cs1 p5cs2/P5CS2 mutant restored early flowering (8.71 ± 0.20 leaves; P < 0.001 vs. wild type and mutant, P < 0.995 vs. flc-7), showing FLC is required for that late-flowering phenotype [4](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants11182348).
- In A. thaliana FRI Sf-2 flc-3, 35S-driven wild-type A. thaliana FLC and the C. rubella MTE allele strongly delayed flowering and repressed FT/SOC1; the C. rubella 1408 allele, which has a splice-site change, delayed flowering only from 25.2 to 29.6 days [5](https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.112.143958) — heterologous C. rubella alleles tested in A. thaliana, not A. thaliana natural variants.

**Limitations**
The association evidence is correlative and partly paradoxical: no significant GWAS signal was found for FLC expression itself, and the FLC–flowering correlation was context-dependent (seen mainly in early-flowering lines at 16 °C; in a greenhouse dataset FLC expression still showed a weak correlation with flowering, and the model predicted 29% of flowering-time variation) [1](https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.118.200571). AtMAD's "TWAS" is a measured expression–phenotype correlation, not genetically predicted expression [2](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaa1042). An extraction note records a weaker-than-anticipated FLC–flowering correlation across 192 accessions, with late-flowering/vernalization-requiring accessions often having low FLC expression and early-flowering accessions high FLC expression; the original full text was unavailable (title-only) [6](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.105.061309). Functional support is gene-specific but comes from induced mutants, transgenes and heterologous C. rubella alleles; among retrieved sources, no experiment tests an A. thaliana natural FLC variant in its native background.

Question: Does Hd1 have the same effect on rice heading across genetic backgrounds, and what evidence explains any differences?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

No — Hd1's effect on heading is strongly background- and day-length-dependent, both in direction and in magnitude.

**Direction can flip with day length and with epistatic partners.** Hd1 (LOC_Os06g16370) [1] is classically bifunctional: it promotes heading under short days but represses it under long days via Hd3a [2](https://doi.org/10.1242/bio.021071)[3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.01827). In the ZS97 background, however, the functional Hd1-ZS97 allele was photoperiod-insensitive and *promoted* heading by 4.64–6.14 days under both natural short- and long-day conditions [2](https://doi.org/10.1242/bio.021071). The authors attribute this to ZS97 carrying a 38.3-kb deletion removing Ghd7: without the Ghd7–Hd1 complex, Hd1's long-day repression activity is lost, and the Hd1–Hd2 interaction disappears [2](https://doi.org/10.1242/bio.021071). Consistently, in a four-gene NIL population, Ghd7/Ghd8 with functional Hd1 produced non-heading under natural long days, and the strongest digenic interaction shifted from Ghd7×Ghd8 (long days) to Ghd7×PRR37 (short days) depending on Hd1 genotype [4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-019-0314-x).

**Magnitude also differs between cultivar backgrounds.** In reciprocal advanced-backcross QTL mapping, Hd1 additive effects on days to heading were detected in the Koshihikari background (≈5.5–7.5 days), but the genetic effect of Hd1 was larger in the IR64 background, which carries functional Hd6 and Hd16; the non-functional hd1 allele is proposed as a major cause of IR64's early heading [5](https://doi.org/10.1270/jsbbs.18172). In temperate japonica, functional Hd1 caused very early, irregular flowering in tropical short days, and loss-of-function hd1 alleles are proposed to have been selected during tropical adaptation [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.01827). A Japanese NIL study reports a late-type Hd1 allele delaying heading by ~13 days in Fusaotome and Chiba 28 backgrounds, but only extraction-level text was available [6](https://doi.org/10.1270/jsbbr.22j15).

**Limitations:** these are different populations, allele types, day lengths and designs, so effect sizes are not directly comparable; the mechanistic explanation (Ghd7-dependent Hd1 function) is supported by genetic and expression evidence, not by a single causal experiment.

Question: How strongly does experimental evidence support a role for natural variation in OsHKT1;5 in rice salt tolerance?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer:
## Short answer

Evidence for OsHKT1;5 (LOC_Os01g20160; also catalogued as SKC1/OsHKT8) as a *functional* salt-tolerance gene is strong, but evidence that **natural allelic variation** at this gene explains rice salt-tolerance differences is moderate and partly conflicting — not uniformly strong.

## What the retrieved records support

**Gene function / necessity (strong, but not natural variation):** CRISPR *hkt1;5* single mutants are salt-sensitive, and the *nac10 hkt1;5* double mutant resembles the single mutant [1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xplc.2026.101771); loss of function triggers massive shoot Na⁺ accumulation [2](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.13595). These establish requirement, not allelic effects.

**Natural-variation evidence (moderate):**
- The salt-tolerance QTL **SKC1**, from the salt-tolerant *indica* Nona Bokra [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1095929), is reported to correspond to OsHKT1;5 and to raise shoot K⁺/Na⁺ [2](https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.13595) — the classic natural-allele basis, but retrieved only as an extraction note/title, and the reference annotation explicitly warns that historical locus names are not proof of interchangeability with the current gene model [4].
- An EcoTILLING association study reported five nonsynonymous SNPs significantly associated with salt-stress traits (e.g. T67K, P140A), with the extracted direction labelled "unclear" [5](https://doi.org/10.1111/pbi.12010).
- A polymorphism survey found more missense variants in tolerant Pokkali than in sensitive IR28 [6](https://doi.org/10.13057/biodiv/d240760) — descriptive, not a tested association.

**Counter-evidence:** In a haplotype analysis of 29 *japonica* accessions, salt-tolerance score did not differ significantly among OsHKT1;5 haplotypes; separately, expression was higher in the tolerant accession Huangluo than in the sensitive Shanfuliya [3](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1095929). Expression–phenotype correlations in an introgression line [7](https://doi.org/10.1186/1939-8433-5-36) are confounded with SOS1/CIPK24/CBL4 co-downregulation.

## Limitations

Some sources were readable only as titles/extraction notes, so exact statistics and allele–trait effect sizes remain unverified; the retrieved set is bounded, not exhaustive.

Question: How strong is the field evidence that DRO1 improves rice yield under drought?
System configuration: PlantQTLdb Assistant (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; literature KG only)
Answer: ## Short answer The field evidence is **real but narrow**: it rests on near-isogenic contrasts in the IR64 background (including the Dro1-NIL field comparison and a further NIL evaluation across three water-management regimes), with independent field validation in elite backgrounds still limited. ## What the retrieved evidence establishes - **Anchor experiment (Uga et al. 2013, Nat Genet):** introducing the *DRO1* (Kinandang Patong) allele into the shallow-rooting cultivar IR64 by backcrossing produced lines that avoided drought through deeper rooting and gave higher yield under drought [1](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2725)[2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-015-0049-2). The primary paper's full text was not available locally (title-level record only), so exact trial numbers, seasons and locations could not be verified here. - **Field conditions and magnitude:** a retrieved full-text article states that under upland conditions with drought stress, Dro1-NIL had a larger root growth angle and **significantly higher grain yield than IR64**; in an irrigated paddy field it also yielded ~10% more, with a suggested contribution from improved post-heading nitrogen uptake from deeper soil [2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12284-015-0049-2). Note the irrigated result is a yield gain *without* drought, not drought-specific benefit; another retrieved literature extraction reports a modest well-watered trade-off [3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44372-026-00844-1), so this well-watered effect is not consistent across sources. - **Additional NIL evaluation:** a separate study of IR64 NILs reported that Dro1-NIL had ~14% higher yield than IR64 across three water-management regimes (flooded lowland, alternate wetting and drying, and rainfed upland), attributed to higher harvest index, aboveground biomass, leaf area index and grain number [4](https://doi.org/10.1080/1343943x.2017.1305868). This adds an experimental comparison but remains in the IR64 background, so it does not supply independent elite-background field validation. - **Independent background:** a Trait Development Pipeline review notes that *dro1* has "thus far mainly been restricted to use in the IR64 background," because the favourable allele is already common in other varieties, and that a set of root QTLs including *dro1* was recently reported to confer a drought yield advantage in the Colombian variety FEDEARROZ 60 (Deshmukh et al. 2024) [5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-025-07399-2). That is a secondary citation; the primary report was not retrieved. - **Pyramiding study (Maudamani):** lines carrying *DRO1* + *DRO3* + *Pup1* out-yielded the recurrent parent, but the reported yield advantage was under **phosphorus-deficient soil**, with normal-P yields at par with the recurrent parent, and three QTLs were co-introgressed, so *DRO1*'s individual drought-yield contribution is not isolated [6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-10951-w). ## Limitations Evidence is largely from near-isogenic/backcross lines rather than released varieties; the drought-yield claim is supported by the Dro1-NIL field comparison plus a further NIL evaluation across water regimes and secondary reviews; multi-season and multi-location replication details were not verifiable from the retrieved text. No retrieved record documents multi-location, multi-season yield trials of *DRO1* alone in diverse elite backgrounds, and the retrieved passages do not establish whether such trials exist. ### Sources - [1](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2725) Control of root system architecture by DEEPER ROOTING 1 increases rice yield under drought conditions..
